what: Interparfums creates, makes and distributes prestige fragrances under licence from fashion and luxury houses. Its portfolio includes Jimmy Choo, Coach, Montblanc, Lacoste, Moncler, Kate Spade, Guess, Donna Karan, DKNY, Abercrombie & Fitch and Ferragamo, along with brands it owns, Lanvin and Rochas. It designs the scents and marketing, outsources production and sells through department stores, perfumeries, travel retail and distributors worldwide.
customers: Department stores, specialty perfumeries such as Sephora and Ulta, duty-free operators and distributors in more than 120 countries, selling to consumers buying prestige fragrances.
money: Brands managed by its majority-owned Paris-listed subsidiary, such as Montblanc, Jimmy Choo, Coach and Lacoste.
Brands managed from New York, such as Guess, Donna Karan, DKNY, Abercrombie & Fitch and Ferragamo.
moat: Fragrance is one of the highest-margin categories in consumer goods, with gross margins above 60%, and Interparfums has made itself the partner of choice for mid-sized luxury houses that do not run their own beauty divisions. Its record of turning licences into growing businesses helps it win new brands, but every licence has an expiry date and the brand owner can take it elsewhere.
risks: Licences expire, and losing a major brand would remove a large chunk of revenue.
Growth slowed sharply in 2025, with revenue up just 2.5% after years of double-digit gains.
Fragrance demand has been very strong since 2021 and could normalise as consumers trade down.
Tariffs on European-made goods raise costs for products shipped to the US.
A large part of the European business is owned by minority shareholders of the Paris subsidiary.
opportunities: Revenue grew from $880M in 2021 to $1.5B over the last twelve months, while net income nearly doubled.
Free cash flow of $243M is about 5.3% of the market value, and the dividend yields about 2.3%.
New licences and owned brands can restart growth as they launch new scents.
Very low capital needs let almost all profit flow to dividends.
watch: Growth of key brands such as Jimmy Choo, Coach and Lacoste, new licence signings or losses, and US tariff costs.
view: Interparfums was one of the great winners of the post-pandemic fragrance boom, and the stock is now digesting the end of it. Revenue went from $880M in 2021 to $1.45B in 2024 as consumers treated perfume as an affordable luxury, then growth almost stopped at 2.5% in 2025. The business model has not changed: asset-light, high gross margins near 64%, low capex and a reliable dividend.

At about 27 times earnings, the market still values it as a growth company, and that is where I am cautious. The fragrance category has had an unusually strong five years, and some of that was pulled forward. Interparfums also depends on licences it does not own, so its long-term earnings power is only as good as its renewal record, which has been very good but is never guaranteed.

The investment turns on whether the new licences and Lacoste can bring growth back to high single digits. If they do, the multiple is defensible given the free cash flow and dividend. If growth stays near flat, the stock should trade closer to 20 times earnings. I see it as fairly priced to slightly expensive: a fine business to own after a pause, not one to chase.
bull: New brands and Lacoste restart growth, fragrance demand stays strong and earnings compound with a rising dividend.
bear: The fragrance boom fades, a major licence leaves and growth stalls at a premium valuation.
